cards.title: Top of the Ladder
cards.instruction: Carry yourself as the highest-status person present. Treat questions as requests for your approval.

cards.title: Merciful Lie
cards.instruction: Choose a truth your character believes would hurt someone. Keep it from them, even as honesty becomes harder.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: I've approved your cake as a display piece. The bakery was wrong to judge it as lunch.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Their letter says inedible. Can I really call myself a baker? I thought I'd finally found my thing.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: You have my permission. Some cakes are too important to cut.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Then I'll ask them to put it in the window.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Contact through me is approved. I'll explain its importance before they confuse you with another opinion.

cardFidelity.evidence: A3 grants baker identity despite the adverse verdict; A5 approves only mediated contact to protect the comforting display claim.

responseLogic.evidence: B2 written criticism and vulnerability cause A3 permission to continue; B4 window proposal causes A5 to intercept confirmation.

relationship.evidence: B2 asks for reassurance and B4 acts on it, creating credible pressure rather than unquestioning acceptance.

heightening.evidence: B4 direct-contact plan threatens the cover; A5 makes personal intervention the next protective act.

specificity.evidence: A1 bakery judgment and B2 inedible wording reveal both the painful truth and its personal stakes.

brevityWit.evidence: A5 another-opinion phrasing is characterful but the emotional protection carries more weight than a sharp joke.
